Browse All Lessons Start Learning How to capture, convert, validate, and securely handle user input in Python. Build interactive CLI tools, robust scripts, and production-ready applications that handle real-world data gracefully — all with step‑by‑step code explanations from @PoeticGlenn. 📖 Introduction Every program that interacts with a human — or with another system — begins with input. Whether you're building a command-line utility, a web API, a data pipeline, or a machine learning model, the way you handle input determines the reliability, security, and usability of your entire application. @PoeticGlenn designed this guide to take you from the simplest input() call to production‑grade CLI tools with argparse, all while teaching you the principles that separate amateur scripts from professional software. Learn to validate, sanitise, and handle input safely — preventing injection, crashes, and data corruption. Build interactive tools that guide users, provide clear feedback, and never crash on bad input. From sys.argv to argparse subcommands — write CLI tools that professionals love. This isn't just a tutorial — it's a complete mental model for thinking about input in Python. Every concept is reinforced with runnable code, step‑by‑step breakdowns, and real‑world patterns you'll use every day. 🐍 🚀 Why Learn This Curriculum If you write code that anyone will ever use — including your future self — you must understand how to handle input correctly. This curriculum, curated by @PoeticGlenn, is not optional; it's foundational. Here's why every developer, regardless of specialisation, needs these skills. Unvalidated input is the #1 cause of vulnerabilities. From SQL injection to buffer overflows, nearly every exploit starts with unsanitised user data. This curriculum teaches you to validate, sanitise, and trust nothing — a mindset that protects every system you build. Whether you do web development, data science, DevOps, embedded systems, or AI — you will handle input. input(), sys.argv, file I/O, environment variables — this curriculum gives you the universal vocabulary to work across stacks. Programs that crash on bad input frustrate users and damage trust. Learning to loop until valid, provide clear error messages, and guide the user transforms a fragile script into a professional tool that people enjoy using. With argparse and sys.argv, you'll build composable, documented, and robust CLI applications that integrate seamlessly with other tools. @PoeticGlenn says: "Input handling is the first line of defence and the first impression of your code. Master it, and everything else becomes easier." 🌍 Significance in the Programming World In the broader programming ecosystem, input handling is not a "nice‑to‑have" — it's a fundamental pillar that separates hobbyist code from enterprise‑grade software. This curriculum, designed by @PoeticGlenn, reflects the patterns and principles used in millions of production systems worldwide. Every data pipeline, ETL job, and analytics workflow starts with input validation. Garbage in, garbage out — this curriculum teaches you to guarantee data quality from the first line. Modern architectures rely on clean, validated input at every boundary. The same principles you learn here — type checking, range validation, parsing — are directly applicable to REST APIs, GraphQL, and gRPC. CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure-as-code, and monitoring tools are all CLI‑first. argparse and sys.argv are the industry standard for building reliable automation scripts. Jump to any section — all entries are equal size 📖 Introduction 🚀 Why Learn This 🌍 Significance ⌨️ input() Basics 🔄 Type Conversion ✅ Input Validation 📦 Multiple Inputs 💻 CLI Arguments ⚙️ argparse Deep Dive 🔒 Secure Input 📂 File Input 🔄 Input in Loops 🛡️ Error Handling 🚀 Real-World Patterns ❓ FAQ 💛 Outro Every interactive Python program starts here. input() reads a line from the user and returns it as a string. The simplest form: call input() with an optional prompt string. The program pauses until the user types something and presses Enter. The returned value is always a string. Step 1: Define the function basic_input_demo() — this groups our code for reuse. Step 2: Call input("What is your name? ") — this displays the prompt and waits for the user to type something and press Enter. Step 3: The value typed by the user is stored in the variable name as a string. Step 4: Use an f-string with print() to display a personalized greeting: f"Hello, {name}!". Step 5: Call input("How old are you? ") to capture the user's age — again stored as a string. Step 6: Display the age back to the user using an f-string. Step 7: Use type(age) to show that input() always returns a string — even for numbers. Step 8: Call the function basic_input_demo() to execute the code. python Copy Run def basic_input_demo(): name = input("What is your name? ") print(f"Hello, {name}! Nice to meet you.") age = input("How old are you? ") print(f"You are {age} years old.") print(f"Type of age: {type(age)}") basic_input_demo() 💡 input() always returns a string. Even if the user types "42", you get "42" — not the integer 42. Conversion is your responsibility. Use triple-quoted strings or 
 for multi-line prompts. This is useful for complex instructions or menus. Step 1: Define a multi-line string using triple quotes """ ... """ — this preserves line breaks. Step 2: Print the multi-line prompt to display a formatted menu or welcome message. Step 3: Call input() three times to capture two numbers and an operation from the user. Step 4: Display the captured inputs back to the user using an f-string. Step 5: Call the function to run the interactive prompt. python Copy Run def multi_line_prompt(): prompt = """ ─── Welcome to the Calculator ─── Enter two numbers and an operation. """ print(prompt) a = input("First number: ") b = input("Second number: ") op = input("Operation (+, -, *, /): ") print(f"Inputs: {a} {op} {b}") multi_line_prompt() If the user just presses Enter without typing anything, input() returns an empty string ''. Always plan for this — many bugs come from assuming input is non-empty. Step 1: Call input() with a prompt asking the user to type something. Step 2: Store the result in response — it could be an empty string if the user pressed Enter. Step 3: Check if response == "" to detect empty input and display a specific message. Step 4: If the input is not empty, display what the user typed. Step 5: Use len(response) to show the character count — 0 for empty input. Step 6: Call the function to test the behavior. python Copy Run def handle_empty(): response = input("Type something (or press Enter): ") if response == "": print("You pressed Enter without typing anything!") else: print(f"You typed: {response}") print(f"Length: {len(response)} characters") handle_empty() ✨ Tip: Use if not response: to check for empty input — it's cleaner than == "". input() always returns a string. To do math, you must convert to int, float, or bool. Use int() to convert a string to an integer. If the string contains non-numeric characters, Python raises a ValueError. Step 1: Call input() to capture a string from the user (age). Step 2: Pass the captured string to int() to convert it to an integer. Step 3: Store the converted integer in the variable age. Step 4: Perform arithmetic — age + 1 calculates next year's age. Step 5: Use type(age) to confirm the variable is now an int. Step 6: Demonstrate int("1010", base=2) to convert a binary string to decimal. Step 7: Call the function to run the code. python Copy Run def int_conversion_demo(): age_str = input("Enter your age: ") age = int(age_str) print(f"Next year you will be {age + 1}") print(f"Type of age: {type(age)}") binary = "1010" decimal = int(binary, base=2) print(f"Binary {binary} = decimal {decimal}") int_conversion_demo() ⚠️ int("3.14") raises ValueError — use float() for decimal numbers, then convert to int if needed. Use float() for numbers with decimals. Accepts strings like "3.14", "-2.5", and "1e-3". Step 1: Call input() with a prompt asking for a price (e.g., "19.99"). Step 2: Use float() to convert the string to a floating-point number. Step 3: Calculate tax as 8% of the price using multiplication: price * 0.08. Step 4: Add the tax to the price to get the total. Step 5: Use f-string formatting with :.2f to display currency with 2 decimal places. Step 6: Use type(price) to confirm the variable is a float. Step 7: Call the function to execute the code. python Copy Run def float_conversion_demo(): price_str = input("Enter the price: $") price = float(price_str) tax = price * 0.08 total = price + tax print(f"Price: ${price:.2f}") print(f"Tax (8%): ${tax:.2f}") print(f"Total: ${total:.2f}") print(f"Type of price: {type(price)}") float_conversion_demo() bool() converts any value to True or False. For strings, only "" is False — all non-empty strings are True. Step 1: Call input() to capture a string from the user. Step 2: Pass the string to bool() to convert it to a boolean. Step 3: Display the boolean result using an f-string. Step 4: Use an if statement to check the boolean value and display a message. Step 5: Show examples of bool(0), bool(42), and bool('yes'). Step 6: Call the function to run the code. python Copy Run def bool_conversion_demo(): user_input = input("Enter something: ") value = bool(user_input) print(f"bool('{user_input}') = {value}") if value: print("You entered something non-empty!") else: print("You entered nothing.") print(f"bool(0) = {bool(0)}") print(f"bool(42) = {bool(42)}") print(f"bool('yes') = {bool('yes')}") bool_conversion_demo() 💡 For user confirmation, check against explicit strings: if response.lower() in ("yes", "y"): rather than relying on bool(). Users make mistakes. Malicious users exploit input. Validate early and often. Wrap conversion in a try/except block to catch invalid input gracefully. Step 1: Define a function validate_integer() to handle validation. Step 2: Inside a try block, call input() and convert with int(). Step 3: If conversion succeeds, print a success message and return the value. Step 4: In the except ValueError block, print an error message and return None. Step 5: Call the function and check if the result is not None before using it. Step 6: If valid, double the number and display it. python Copy Run def validate_integer(): try: value = int(input("Enter a whole number: ")) print(f"✅ You entered: {value}") return value except ValueError: print("❌ That's not a valid whole number!") return None result = validate_integer() if result is not None: print(f"Double it: {result * 2}") Keep asking until the user provides valid input. This pattern is essential for interactive CLI tools. Step 1: Define get_positive_number(prompt) that loops until valid input is received. Step 2: Inside an infinite while True loop, attempt to convert the input to float. Step 3: If conversion succeeds and the value is positive, return the value (exits the function). Step 4: If the value is not positive, show an error message and continue the loop. Step 5: If conversion fails with ValueError, show an error and continue. Step 6: In main(), call the function with a prompt and calculate the area of a circle. Step 7: Display the calculated area with 2 decimal places. python Copy Run def get_positive_number(prompt: str) -> float: while True: try: value = float(input(prompt)) if value > 0: return value print("❌ Please enter a positive number.") except ValueError: print("❌ Invalid input. Please enter a number.") def main(): radius = get_positive_number("Enter radius: ") area = 3.14159 * radius ** 2 print(f"✅ Area of circle: {area:.2f}") main() 💡 The while True + return pattern is the cleanest way to loop until valid input is received. No messy flag variables. Sometimes you need a number within a specific range (e.g., 1–100, 0–10). Add bounds checking after conversion. Step 1: Define get_score() that validates a score between 0 and 100. Step 2: Inside the loop, attempt to convert input to int. Step 3: Check if the score is between 0 and 100 inclusive — if so, return it. Step 4: If out of range, show a message and continue the loop. Step 5: Define grade_score() that returns a letter grade based on the score. Step 6: Call get_score() to get a valid score, then pass it to grade_score(). Step 7: Display the score and its corresponding grade. python Copy Run def get_score() -> int: while True: try: score = int(input("Enter a score (0–100): ")) if 0 <= score <= 100: return score print("❌ Score must be between 0 and 100.") except ValueError: print("❌ Please enter a whole number.") def grade_score(score: int) -> str: if score >= 90: return "A" if score >= 80: return "B" if score >= 70: return "C" if score >= 60: return "D" return "F" score = get_score() print(f"✅ Score {score} → Grade {grade_score(score)}") Validate strings for length, allowed characters, or pattern matching with regex. Step 1: Import the re module for regular expression matching. Step 2: Define validate_name() that loops until a valid name is entered. Step 3: Use len() to check that the name is between 2 and 30 characters. Step 4: Use re.match() with a pattern to ensure only letters, spaces, hyphens, and apostrophes. Step 5: Define validate_email() that loops until a valid email is entered. Step 6: Use a regex pattern to check the email format (basic validation). Step 7: Call both validation functions and display a welcome message. python Copy Run import re def validate_name() -> str: while True: name = input("Enter your name (2–30 letters): ").strip() if len(name) < 2 or len(name) > 30: print("❌ Name must be 2–30 characters.") continue if not re.match(r"^[A-Za-z\s\-'']+$", name): print("❌ Name contains invalid characters.") continue return name def validate_email() -> str: while True: email = input("Enter your email: ").strip() if re.match(r"^[\w\.-]+@[\w\.-]+\.\w+$", email): return email print("❌ Invalid email format.") name = validate_name() email = validate_email() print(f"✅ Welcome, {name}! Email: {email}") ✨ Use str.strip() to remove accidental leading/trailing spaces before validation. Sometimes you need to collect multiple values in a single line, or ask for a list of items. Use str.split() to break a single input line into multiple pieces. Then convert each piece individually. Step 1: Call input() to capture a line with three numbers separated by spaces. Step 2: Use split() to break the string into a list of parts. Step 3: Check that exactly three parts were entered — if not, show an error and return. Step 4: Convert each part to float inside a try/except block. Step 5: Calculate the sum and average of the three numbers. Step 6: Display the results with 2 decimal places. python Copy Run def parse_multiple_numbers(): raw = input("Enter three numbers separated by spaces: ") parts = raw.split() print(f"Parts: {parts}") if len(parts) != 3: print("❌ Please enter exactly three numbers.") return try: a, b, c = float(parts[0]), float(parts[1]), float(parts[2]) print(f"✅ Sum: {a + b + c:.2f}") print(f"✅ Average: {(a + b + c) / 3:.2f}") except ValueError: print("❌ All inputs must be numbers.") parse_multiple_numbers() Use a loop to collect items until the user signals they are done (e.g., with a blank line or a sentinel value). Step 1: Define collect_items() that returns a list of strings. Step 2: Print instructions for the user: enter items one per line, press Enter twice to finish. Step 3: Inside an infinite loop, call input() to get each line. Step 4: If the line is empty (""), break out of the loop. Step 5: Otherwise, append the line to the items list. Step 6: In main(), display the collected items with numbers. Step 7: Call the function to run the interactive collection. python Copy Run def collect_items() -> list: items = [] print("Enter items one per line. Press Enter twice to finish.") while True: line = input("> ") if line == "": break items.append(line) return items def main(): items = collect_items() print(f"
You entered {len(items)} items:") for i, item in enumerate(items, 1): print(f" {i}. {item}") main() 💡 The double-Enter pattern is a common UX pattern for CLI tools that collect lists of items. It's clean, intuitive, and works everywhere. Input isn't just interactive — many Python scripts are called with arguments from the shell. sys.argv is a list of all command-line arguments passed to the script. The first element sys.argv[0] is the script name itself. Step 1: Import the sys module to access command-line arguments. Step 2: Define show_argv() to display all arguments. Step 3: sys.argv[0] is always the script name (preset in this environment). Step 4: len(sys.argv) - 1 gives the number of arguments passed. Step 5: Use enumerate(sys.argv[1:], 1) to loop through each argument. Step 6: If there is at least one argument, display the first one. Step 7: Call the function to show the arguments. python Copy Run import sys def show_argv(): print(f"Script name: {sys.argv[0]}") print(f"Number of arguments: {len(sys.argv) - 1}") for i, arg in enumerate(sys.argv[1:], 1): print(f" Arg {i}: {arg}") if len(sys.argv) > 1: print(f"
First argument: {sys.argv[1]}") show_argv() ⚠️ In this browser sandbox, sys.argv is preset to ['script.py', 'Alice', '28'] so the demo has something to show. In a real terminal, it reflects the arguments you typed. For simple scripts, manually parse sys.argv. Check the number of arguments and handle each position. Step 1: Import sys for command-line access. Step 2: Check if fewer than 2 arguments were provided — show usage message if so. Step 3: sys.argv[1] is the first argument (the name). Step 4: Check if a second argument (age) was provided — if so, try to convert to int. Step 5: If conversion fails, set age to "invalid". Step 6: Display a greeting with the name and age. Step 7: Call the function to demonstrate. python Copy Run import sys def simple_cli(): if len(sys.argv) < 2: print("Usage: python script.py <name> [age]") return name = sys.argv[1] age = "unknown" if len(sys.argv) >= 3: try: age = int(sys.argv[2]) except ValueError: age = "invalid" print(f"Hello, {name}!") print(f"Age: {age}") simple_cli() For robust, production-ready CLI tools, argparse is the standard library module that handles flags, options, subcommands, and help text automatically. Define arguments, flags, and options with type checking and automatic help generation. Step 1: Import the argparse module. Step 2: Create an ArgumentParser instance with a description. Step 3: Add a positional argument: "name" — this is required. Step 4: Add an optional argument: "--age" with type int and default 18. Step 5: Add a flag: "--verbose" with action="store_true". Step 6: Parse arguments with parser.parse_args(), passing an explicit list of fake CLI arguments rather than reading real argv. Step 7: Access values via args.name, args.age, args.verbose. Step 8: Display the parsed values and check if the user is an adult. python Copy Run import argparse def build_parser(): parser = argparse.ArgumentParser( description="A simple CLI tool with argparse" ) parser.add_argument("name", help="Your name") parser.add_argument("--age", type=int, default=18, help="Your age (default: 18)") parser.add_argument("--verbose", action="store_true", help="Enable verbose output") return parser def main(): parser = build_parser() args = parser.parse_args(["Alice", "--age", "25", "--verbose"]) if args.verbose: print("🔍 Verbose mode enabled") print(f"Hello, {args.name}!") print(f"Age: {args.age}") if args.age >= 18: print("✅ You are an adult.") else: print("🔞 You are a minor.") main() 💡 argparse automatically generates --help output, validates types, and provides error messages for invalid input. Note we pass an explicit list to parse_args() instead of reading real sys.argv — this keeps the demo self-contained and avoids SystemExit surprises. Positional arguments are required and ordered. Optional arguments are prefixed with -- and can appear anywhere. Step 1: Create a parser with a description for file operations. Step 2: Add "source" as a required positional argument. Step 3: Add "dest" as an optional positional with nargs="?" and a default value. Step 4: Add "-v" / "--verbose" as a flag (store_true). Step 5: Add "-f" / "--force" as a flag (store_true). Step 6: Parse arguments with an explicit fake-argument list. Step 7: Display all parsed values to show how each argument is handled. python Copy Run import argparse def create_parser(): parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="File operations") parser.add_argument("source", help="Source file path") parser.add_argument("dest", nargs="?", default=".", help="Destination path (default: current dir)") parser.add_argument("-v", "--verbose", action="store_true", help="Verbose output") parser.add_argument("-f", "--force", action="store_true", help="Overwrite without asking") return parser def main(): parser = create_parser() args = parser.parse_args(["report.txt", "/backup/", "--verbose"]) print(f"Source: {args.source}") print(f"Destination: {args.dest}") print(f"Verbose: {args.verbose}") print(f"Force: {args.force}") main() Never echo passwords to the screen. Use getpass for secure, hidden input. This function works like input() but doesn't echo characters to the console. Perfect for passwords, API keys, and sensitive data. Step 1: Import the getpass module. Step 2: Use input() for the username (visible input). Step 3: Use getpass.getpass() for the password (hidden input — in this browser sandbox it's mocked with a JS prompt dialog). Step 4: Display the username and the length of the password (not the password itself). Step 5: Check if the credentials match a hardcoded pair and display success or failure. Step 6: Call the function to test secure login. python Copy Run import getpass def secure_login(): username = input("Username: ") password = getpass.getpass("Password: ") print(f"
Username: {username}") print(f"Password length: {len(password)} characters (hidden)") if username == "admin" and password == "secret123": print("✅ Login successful!") else: print("❌ Invalid credentials.") secure_login() ⚠️ In this browser sandbox, getpass is mocked using a JavaScript prompt() dialog (it still doesn't echo into the page output). In a local terminal, the real getpass hides typed characters entirely. When creating new passwords, ask twice and compare. This prevents typos and ensures accuracy. Step 1: Import getpass for hidden input. Step 2: Ask for the current password using getpass(). Step 3: Check if the current password matches the expected value. Step 4: Ask for the new password twice using getpass(). Step 5: Compare the two new passwords — if they don't match, show an error. Step 6: Check if the new password is at least 8 characters long. Step 7: If all checks pass, confirm the password change. python Copy Run import getpass def change_password(): print("🔐 Change Password") print("-" * 30) current = getpass.getpass("Current password: ") if current != "secret123": print("❌ Incorrect current password.") return new1 = getpass.getpass("New password: ") new2 = getpass.getpass("Confirm new password: ") if new1 != new2: print("❌ Passwords do not match.") return if len(new1) < 8: print("❌ Password must be at least 8 characters.") return print("✅ Password changed successfully!") change_password() Sometimes input comes from a file, not from a user typing. Learn to read structured data from CSV, JSON, and text files. Use open() with a context manager to read files safely. Always specify encoding. Step 1: Define read_text_file(path) that attempts to read a file. Step 2: Use open() with "r" mode and encoding="utf-8" inside a with block. Step 3: Read the entire file content with f.read(). Step 4: Display the file path, character count, and first 200 characters. Step 5: Catch FileNotFoundError and display a friendly error. Step 6: Catch any other exceptions and display the error. Step 7: Call the function with a sample file path that this environment pre-creates for you. python Copy Run def read_text_file(path: str): try: with open(path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f: content = f.read() print(f"📄 File: {path}") print(f"Characters: {len(content)}") print("Content:") print(content[:200]) except FileNotFoundError: print(f"❌ File not found: {path}") except Exception as e: print(f"❌ Error reading file: {e}") read_text_file("sample.txt") ✨ This environment pre-creates sample.txt in the virtual filesystem before your code runs, so this demo works out of the box. In a local environment, it reads from the actual filesystem. Use the csv module to read structured tabular data with proper quoting and escaping. Step 1: Import the csv module and StringIO for in-memory parsing. Step 2: Define parse_csv_data(csv_text) that takes a CSV string. Step 3: Create a DictReader from StringIO(csv_text). Step 4: Convert the reader to a list of dictionaries (rows). Step 5: Display the number of rows and the column names. Step 6: Loop through the first 3 rows and print each row. Step 7: Define a sample CSV string and call the function. python Copy Run import csv from io import StringIO def parse_csv_data(csv_text: str): reader = csv.DictReader(StringIO(csv_text)) rows = list(reader) print(f"📊 Found {len(rows)} rows") if rows: print(f"Columns: {', '.join(rows[0].keys())}") for row in rows[:3]: print(row) csv_sample = """name,age,city Alice,30,New York Bob,25,London Charlie,35,Paris""" parse_csv_data(csv_sample) JSON is the most common format for APIs and configuration. Use json.load() or json.loads(). Step 1: Import the json module. Step 2: Define a sample JSON string (not a dict) with user data. Step 3: Define parse_json(data) that parses a JSON string. Step 4: Use json.loads() to convert the string to a Python dictionary. Step 5: Access values using dictionary keys: obj["user"], obj["level"], etc. Step 6: Calculate the average of the scores list. Step 7: Catch JSONDecodeError for invalid JSON. python Copy Run import json json_sample = '{"user": "glenn", "level": "advanced", "scores": [95, 88, 92]}' def parse_json(data: str): try: obj = json.loads(data) print("✅ JSON parsed successfully") print(f"User: {obj['user']}") print(f"Level: {obj['level']}") print(f"Scores: {obj['scores']}") print(f"Average: {sum(obj['scores']) / len(obj['scores']):.1f}") except json.JSONDecodeError as e: print(f"❌ Invalid JSON: {e}") parse_json(json_sample) ⚠️ The sample JSON is a string (single-quoted in Python), not a dict literal — json.loads() requires a string argument. Many programs need to keep asking for input until a condition is met. Master the interactive loop. Use a sentinel value (like "quit" or 0) to let the user exit the loop. Step 1: Define sentinel_loop() with total and count variables. Step 2: Print instructions: type "quit" to stop. Step 3: Inside while True, call input() and store in raw. Step 4: Check if raw.lower() == "quit" — if so, break the loop. Step 5: Try to convert raw to float — if successful, add to total and increment count. Step 6: If conversion fails, show an error and continue. Step 7: After the loop, display the summary if any numbers were entered. python Copy Run def sentinel_loop(): total = 0 count = 0 print("Enter numbers to sum. Type 'quit' to stop.") while True: raw = input("> ") if raw.lower() == "quit": break try: num = float(raw) total += num count += 1 print(f"✅ Added {num}. Running total: {total:.2f}") except ValueError: print("❌ Invalid number. Try again.") if count > 0: print(f"📊 Summary: {count} numbers, total {total:.2f}, average {total/count:.2f}") else: print("No numbers entered.") sentinel_loop() A menu-driven program lets the user choose actions repeatedly until they decide to exit. Step 1: Define show_menu() that prints the menu options. Step 2: Define menu_loop() with an infinite loop. Step 3: Call show_menu() and capture the user's choice. Step 4: If choice is "0", print goodbye and break. Step 5: If choice is "1", ask for a name and greet the user. Step 6: If choice is "2", ask for a number and double it. Step 7: If choice is "3", import time and show the current time. Step 8: For any other choice, show an error message. python Copy Run def show_menu(): print("
📋 Menu") print(" 1. Say hello") print(" 2. Double a number") print(" 3. Show current time") print(" 0. Exit") def menu_loop(): while True: show_menu() choice = input("Choose an option: ").strip() if choice == "0": print("👋 Goodbye!") break elif choice == "1": name = input("Your name: ") print(f"Hello, {name}! 👋") elif choice == "2": try: num = float(input("Enter a number: ")) print(f"Double: {num * 2}") except ValueError: print("❌ Invalid number.") elif choice == "3": import time print(f"🕐 {time.strftime('%H:%M:%S')}") else: print("❌ Invalid option. Try again.") menu_loop() 💡 Menu-driven programs are the backbone of many CLI utilities. The pattern scales well with functions for each option. Anticipate every possible failure and handle it gracefully — your users will thank you. Build a reusable validation function that handles multiple failure modes and provides clear feedback. Step 1: Import Optional from typing for type hints. Step 2: Define safe_int_input() with parameters for prompt, min, max, and retries. Step 3: Loop for the specified number of retries. Step 4: Inside each attempt, try to convert the input to int. Step 5: Check if the value is within the specified min and max bounds. Step 6: If valid, return the value immediately. Step 7: If invalid or conversion fails, show an error and continue. Step 8: After all retries, return None. Step 9: Test the function with age and score inputs. python Copy Run from typing import Optional def safe_int_input( prompt: str, min_val: Optional[int] = None, max_val: Optional[int] = None, retries: int = 3 ) -> Optional[int]: for attempt in range(1, retries + 1): try: raw = input(f"{prompt} ") value = int(raw) if min_val is not None and value < min_val: print(f"❌ Value must be at least {min_val}.") continue if max_val is not None and value > max_val: print(f"❌ Value must be at most {max_val}.") continue return value except ValueError: print(f"❌ Invalid integer. ({retries - attempt} attempts left)") print("❌ Too many attempts. Returning None.") return None age = safe_int_input("Enter your age:", min_val=1, max_val=120) if age is not None: print(f"✅ Age: {age}") score = safe_int_input("Enter a score (0-100):", min_val=0, max_val=100) if score is not None: print(f"✅ Score: {score}") When reading files, use with to guarantee the file is closed even if an exception occurs. Step 1: Define read_file_safely(path) that attempts to read a file. Step 2: Use with open() to open the file — this automatically closes it. Step 3: Read the content and return it. Step 4: Catch FileNotFoundError and display a specific error. Step 5: Catch PermissionError for access issues. Step 6: Catch UnicodeDecodeError for encoding problems. Step 7: Catch any other unexpected exceptions with a generic handler. Step 8: Call the function and check if content was read successfully. python Copy Run def read_file_safely(path: str): try: with open(path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f: return f.read() except FileNotFoundError: print(f"❌ File not found: {path}") return None except PermissionError: print(f"❌ Permission denied: {path}") return None except UnicodeDecodeError as e: print(f"❌ Encoding error: {e}") return None except Exception as e: print(f"❌ Unexpected error: {e}") return None content = read_file_safely("sample.txt") if content is not None: print(f"✅ Read {len(content)} characters") Putting it all together — input handling patterns used in production Python applications. Every major CLI tool — git, docker, pip — uses this pattern. Common questions about Python input, answered. + Python is strongly typed and does not auto-convert. This design makes the program's behaviour predictable and explicit. You — the programmer — decide what type the input should be and convert it accordingly. + Wrap int() or float() in a try/except block. For user-facing programs, loop until valid input is received. Never assume input will be correct. + sys.argv is a raw list of arguments. argparse is a full-featured parser that handles flags, options, type conversion, help generation, and error messages. Use argparse for any non-trivial CLI tool. + input() reads the entire line, including spaces. For multiple values on one line, use split() and then process each piece. For multi-line input, collect in a loop until a sentinel value is entered. + getpass is safe for hiding input from shoulder surfers, but it does not encrypt the input. Use it for passwords in local scripts. For production applications, use environment variables or dedicated secret management tools. + Python 3 handles Unicode strings by default. input() returns a str that can contain any Unicode character. When reading from files, always specify encoding="utf-8". + Use a regular expression for basic format validation. For production, consider using a dedicated library like email-validator. Never try to fully validate an email address with regex alone — send a confirmation link to verify.
